newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl wants no preconditions for SPD tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl wants no preconditions for SPD tax talks.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said his ruling coalition would only resume cross-party talks on major tax reforms without preconditions from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), a German newspaper said on Saturday.

According a report in Welt am Sonntag released ahead of publication on Sunday, Kohl said his coalition, which includes his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and junior partner the Free Democrats (FDP), would agree to a new round of talks before the Easter holiday next weekend.

But, Kohl said, "we will not allow any preconditions" for resuming the talks aimed at passing tax reform measures needed to help whip Germany's finances into shape for European currency union that is slated to start in January 1999.

The SPD pulled out of the tax talks with the coalition in a recent clash over coal subsidy cuts, and has not yet agreed to return to the negotiating table. The party can block most tax measures through its majority in the upper house of parliament.
"I would hope and trust that the Social Democrats would have the rational power to see these issues through," Kohl said, noting the SPD has not ruled out pension reform talks.
Kohl's comments echoed those of Finance Minister Theo Waigel, who said in an interview with the Austrian daily newspaper Kurier on Saturday the SPD was the "most backward" political party in Europe.

Waigel again called on the SPD to return to the negotiating table. He also said on Friday that "the delaying tactics of the SPD are harming the common good, the unemployed and those in Germany who still have work".

The 1998 tax bill envisages cutting corporate and commercial income tax and unifying them at a common 40 percent rate in a revenue-neutral measure which would be offset by tightening up on corporate write-off possibilities.

The bill would also cut two points off the solidarity income tax surcharge to 5.5 percent, cutting 7.5 billion marks off the tax burden. The lion's share of income and corporate tax cuts would come in separate legislation for 1999.

Waigel said it would be possible with SPD cooperation to pass the bill by July, and a 1999 tax bill by the end of the year, giving "a decisive push for a positive change of climate for doing business in Germany". -- John Gilardi, Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
